articles.title: 'What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable': Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row on stage
articles.summary: US News: Ed Sheeran on Saturday addressed the controversy surrounding rapper Macklemore's removal from his US tour, saying he could no longer “hide” how he fee.
articles.body: Ed Sheeran on Saturday addressed the controversy surrounding rapper Macklemore's removal from his US tour, saying he could no longer “hide” how he feels about the Israel-Palestine conflict.The controversy began after Macklemore made pro-Palestinian remarks during Sheeran’s September 4 and 5 shows at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, including saying “Free Palestine” and performing his protest song “Hind’s Hall”.Speaking at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field, Sheeran opened his solo concert by addressing the controversy and the wider debate over free speech that has engulfed his Loop Tour.Sheeran said he wanted his music and concerts to focus on unity and humanity rather than politics. However, he said the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel were horrific, while describing the situation in Gaza as “catastrophic and unjustifiable.”“I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet,” Sheeran said.He acknowledged that he had made “mistakes” while navigating the difficult decisions surrounding the controversy. “My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone,” he said, adding that he remained committed to his fans, according to BBC.“Now, I want to address the question of where I stand in the situation in Israel and Palestine, and whether my doing this concert here tonight implies where I stand,” he said.“I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division; about humanity, not politics. But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore," he added.'What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic'Sheeran further described the October 7, 2023 attacks in Israel as “horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain”.“What happened in Israel and at the Nome Museum Festival on October 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain,” Sheeran said.“What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate. My heart has been broken by the scale of of devastation and loss of civilian lives, of children's lives, and this systemic injustice we're seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked,” he added.Sheeran said he was trying “to work out how to make a contribution that helps victims of these terrible times and listening and learning, because I do not know enough”.He also said he was “deeply worried about the idea that venues pre-approve content for performance”. The singer ended his remarks by saying he wanted his concerts to remain spaces where people with opposing views could come together.“I am honestly so grateful that you're here tonight with me,” he told the audience. “This concert is still a place where everyone is welcome and everyone here can stand beside people that have opposing views,” he added.Macklemore was subsequently removed from the remaining US dates after venues objected to his participation, according to the tour promoter. Several supporting acts later withdrew from the tour in solidarity.Why was Macklemore removed?Macklemore’s remarks drew criticism from some Jewish and pro-Israel organisations, with the Israeli-American Council calling for him to be removed from the tour.Messina Touring Group, the promoter behind the US leg of Sheeran’s Loop Tour, later announced that Macklemore would no longer perform on the remaining dates.The promoter said venues had informed it that they would not allow concerts featuring the rapper to proceed, potentially leading to cancellations affecting hundreds of thousands of ticket holders.Sheeran has said the decision was made by the promoter and venues, not by him. He also expressed concern about venues deciding in advance what performers can say on stage.Macklemore has said the decision came after pressure from venue owners, including Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and Gillette Stadium, where Sheeran was scheduled to perform.Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the rapper of hate speech and said he was “only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas”.The controversy intensified after several artists withdrew from Sheeran’s tour in solidarity with Macklemore. Irish singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe, Danish band Lukas Graham and members of Sheeran’s touring band Beoga were among those who pulled out.Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, also withdrew from the South American leg of the tour. The artists cited concerns about freedom of speech and the decision to remove Macklemore.Macklemore later said he and Sheeran had held “difficult conversations” following the MetLife shows. He maintained his support for Palestinians and said he did not regret using the tour stage to speak about the conflict.Macklemore said Wednesday that he would donate $1 million to Palestinian relief efforts and called on Kraft to match the contribution.Despite the controversy, several fans attending Sheeran’s Philadelphia concert said they continued to support the singer. Some said they had hesitated about attending because of the dispute but ultimately chose to go ahead with the show.Others attended a protest outside the stadium instead, while some fans said they wanted to put the controversy aside and enjoy the music. Reuters reported that fans at the concert largely expressed support for Sheeran despite the backlash.Pro-Palestinian protesters also gathered outside Lincoln Financial Field ahead of the concert, criticising Macklemore’s removal from the tour. Sheeran’s Loop Tour is scheduled to continue with shows across North and South America.Gaza death tollIsraeli airstrikes killed at least three Palestinians in the Gaza Strip on Saturday, according to health officials. One strike near the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza killed Basir Al-Bursh, the son of Munir Al-Bursh, director-general of Gaza’s health ministry, medics and family members said.Palestinian authorities say more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s assault on Gaza, which began after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel in October 2023.A US-brokered ceasefire agreed last year calls for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but little progress has been made as negotiators remain divided over Hamas disarming and Israel withdrawing its troops.More than 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect, according to territory health officials. The Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed during the same period.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Maharashtra minister's niece Nila Vikhe Patil elected to Swedish Parliament
articles.summary: Europe News: Nila Vikhe Patil, daughter of Maharashtra educationist Ashok Vikhe Patil, was elected to the Swedish Parliament on Saturday from the Stockholm City co.
articles.body: Nila Vikhe Patil, daughter of Maharashtra educationist Ashok Vikhe Patil, was elected to the Swedish Parliament on Saturday from the Stockholm City constituency.Nila is the great-granddaughter of the founder of Asia’s first cooperative sugar factory, Vithalrao Vikhe Patil, and granddaughter of late Union minister Balasaheb Vikhe Patil. Her uncle, Radhakrishna Vikhe Patil, is a Maharashtra minister.Born in Sweden, Nila spent her early years in Ahmednagar, Maharashtra. She holds a bachelor’s degree and an MBA from the Gothenburg School of Business, with Economics and Law, and also studied for an MBA at the University of Complutense in Madrid.Since 2020, she has worked at PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), a global services network, offering strategy, management, technology and risk consulting.In April 2025, she became an authorised public accountant.She has been a member of the Stockholm City Council. She also served as a political adviser in the Swedish Prime Minister’s Office, focusing on finance, taxes and housing during the Stefan Lofven administration.“It feels nice to be a part of the 349-member Parliament. I am looking forward to contributing to the city and the country,” Nila told news agency PTI.“I would like to be a voice for those who cannot vote,” she said. “I want to contribute to a society where every child gets a chance for a good future. We need a habitable planet with clean water, living nature and as few human-caused natural disasters as possible,” she added.The 41-year-old Nila said that she loves India dearly and misses her grandfather a lot.“I hope to make my grandfather proud. He made me read the state budget when I was 15,” Nila said.“I love India dearly and I feel very connected. I have lots of close Indian friends. I miss my grandfather a lot. He used to call me almost weekly during his last years,” she added.Sweden’s left-leaning opposition won a narrow majority in the September 13 election. The Swedish Election Authority said the four opposition parties won 176 seats in the 349-seat Riksdag (Parliament). The four parties that make up or support the outgoing conservative-led government took 173 seats.The opposition Green Party is focused on environmentalism, renewable energy and green politics.Nila has been active in the Green Party for 25 years and is a member of the Election Committee of the Stockholm Green Party.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Ride or Die' Season 2 starring Octavia Spencer and Hannah Waddingham gets cancelled after one season
articles.summary: News News: 'Ride or Die', starring Octavia Spencer and Hannah Waddingham, has been cancelled after one season, prompting speculation about the future of the series. Although the show may find a new buyer, Season 2 remains uncertain.
articles.body: 'Ride or Die' has run into an unexpected roadblock. The action-comedy starring Octavia Spencer and Hannah Waddingham has been cancelled after just one season, leaving fans wondering if they have seen the last of Debbie Claybourne and Judith Burton.There is a little hope for the show, though. Deadline reported that the studio is looking to shop the series to other buyers. So, while 'Ride or Die' Season 2 is not happening right now, the story may not be finished.The show premiered on Prime Video on July 15, 2026, with all eight episodes released together. It picked up attention during its short run, particularly for the pairing of Spencer and Waddingham and the show's mix of comedy, action and friendship.What is 'Ride or Die' about?The series follows Debbie Claybourne and Judith Burton, two best friends who suddenly find themselves in a very messy situation when a huge secret comes out. Debbie, played by Octavia Spencer, thinks she knows Judith pretty well. Then she discovers that her best friend has actually been living a secret life as an international assassin.Things get even worse when one of Judith's assignments goes wrong. Before long, the two women are running across Europe and trying to stay ahead of the danger chasing them.That setup gives 'Ride or Die' a little bit of everything. There is action, there is comedy and, underneath all of it, there is the friendship between two women who are suddenly forced to look at each other very differently.Paramount Television Studios' official announcement described the series as an action-comedy centred on two best friends whose lives are turned upside down after Judith's secret world collides with Debbie's ordinary life.Octavia Spencer and Hannah Waddingham led the castA big part of the appeal of 'Ride or Die' was seeing Octavia Spencer and Hannah Waddingham share the screen. Spencer plays Debbie, while Waddingham plays Judith. The two actresses also served as executive producers on the series.The cast also includes Ed Skrein, Cal Lynch, Savannah Steyn, Jamie Parker, Jacky Ido, Sylvia Hoeks and Bill Nighy. The friendship between Spencer and Waddingham was also something they talked about around the show's release. Speaking with the Los Angeles Times, the actresses discussed their friendship and what it was like working together on the series.Behind the camera, Tessa Coates created 'Ride or Die', with Matt Miller serving as showrunner. Peyton Reed directed the series.Why did 'Ride or Die' get cancelled?There has been no specific explanation for why 'Ride or Die' was cancelled. And the cancellation is a little surprising when you look at how the show performed early on. Deadline reported that Luminate recorded 927,000 views for the series during its first two days.Nielsen also reported 869 million viewing minutes during its first week. According to Deadline, the series reached No. 8 among overall titles and No. 3 among original programs during that period. It continued to perform strongly during its second week as well.Still, good reviews and a strong start do not always translate into another season. The decision to renew a series can involve its viewing numbers, how long people keep watching, production costs and what a platform wants its upcoming lineup to look like. In this case, the studio is reportedly trying to find another home for 'Ride or Die'. Whether that actually happens is another question. There is no confirmed buyer or Season 2 order yet.If the series does find another buyer, Spencer and Waddingham could potentially return as Debbie and Judith for another season. But until a new home and an official renewal are announced, 'Ride or Die' Season 2 remains uncertain. For now, fans will have to wait and see whether this is really the end of Debbie and Judith's chaotic ride.

articles.title: Tunisian protesters demand release of four Sumud activists
articles.summary: The protest comes as the health of one detainee deteriorates after more than a month on hunger strike.
articles.body:
Tunis, Tunisia – Dozens of people protested in Tunis on Saturday demanding the release of four Global Sumud Flotilla activists, as concern mounts over their deteriorating health after one of them entered his second month of a hunger strike.

The protesters marched from the headquarters of the Tunisian National Journalists’ Union (SNJT) to Avenue Habib Bourguiba in central Tunis, carrying Tunisian and Palestinian flags and portraits of the four detainees and calling for their release and an end to the case against them.

They also chanted anti-government slogans, including: “No fear, no terror, the street belongs to the people”, “Down with the president’s repression, down with the oppression of the people”, and “Your narrative is a Zionist one, you agents of imperialism.”

The demonstration came days after a court extended the pre-trial detention of Wael Naouar, Ghassen Henchiri, Ghassen Boughdiri and Nabil Channoufi by another four months. They have been held since March in an investigation into alleged financial irregularities linked to fundraising for the flotilla, according to Tunisian state media, citing judicial sources.

The four activists and their defence team deny wrongdoing, while supporters say the case is part of a wider crackdown on civil society and political dissent.

Naouar, a member of the flotilla’s steering committee, began an open-ended hunger strike on August 16 to protest his detention. The other three joined him on September 9, according to statements from supporters and the Global Sumud Flotilla.

Ghassen Bouaazi, a member of the National Committee for the Defence of Sumud Flotilla Activists, said Naouar’s health had deteriorated significantly.

“Wael Naouar has been on hunger strike for about 35 days and his health has deteriorated considerably,” Bouaazi told Al Jazeera on the sidelines of Saturday’s protest.

He said Naouar had experienced repeated fainting, difficulty breathing and hallucinations and had lost more than 20kg (44lb).

“There is now a real danger threatening him,” Bouaazi said, adding that the committee holds President Kais Saied and his government politically, legally and morally responsible for any harm that might come to the detainees.

“We demand that the authorities close this case once and for all,” Bouaazi said, describing the accusations against the four activists as “dubious claims”.

He described the arrests as part of what he called a broader campaign targeting political activists, journalists, rights defenders and trade unionists, saying similar financial crime and money laundering allegations had been used in other cases.

He said the case was unfolding within “a judicial system that is not independent and is subject to the executive branch’s monopoly”.

Bouaazi said the committee believes the prosecution of the flotilla activists is aimed at criminalising independent popular solidarity with Palestinians and is part of what he described as an increasingly security-focused approach to protests and public life in Tunisia.

The four activists are members of the Global Sumud Flotilla, an international campaign that sought to challenge Israel’s blockade of Gaza and deliver humanitarian aid.

The latest demonstration follows a statement issued on Tuesday by former members of Tunisia’s General Students Union (UGET) and activists from different generations of the student movement, who called for the immediate release of the four detainees, including Naouar, a former secretary-general of UGET.

The group said Saied and his government were responsible for the safety of the hunger strikers and urged student, trade union, rights and civil society groups to mobilise around the detainees’ case.

According to Nidhal Khadraoui, another former secretary-general of UGET, Naouar and the other activists remain determined to continue their hunger strike until their release.

Khadraoui also said Henchiri is in urgent need of surgery following complications from a previous injury he sustained during his detention in Israel, but that the procedure has not been carried out despite a prison doctor’s recommendation.

Supporters of the Global Sumud Flotilla have also rallied, calling for the immediate release of the “Sumud four” and saying their continued detention has become a focus of international concern.

The case comes amid broader concerns from rights groups about the shrinking space for civil society in Tunisia.

Human Rights Watch said Tunisian authorities have increasingly used financial, anti-money laundering and counterterrorism legislation against civil society actors and activists. The group has also criticised Saied for concentrating power in the presidency since 2021, weakening parliament and undermining judicial independence, and has raised concerns about the use of prolonged pre-trial detention.

Saied’s government has rejected accusations that the judiciary is being used to silence opponents, saying the judiciary is independent and legal proceedings are conducted according to the law.

“The Tunisian state, acting on behalf of the Zionist entity, is punishing our comrades for their struggle for Gaza and Palestine,” Khadraoui told Al Jazeera.

“All upcoming actions will be escalatory, and we hold Kais Saied’s authorities fully responsible for putting our comrades in prison,” he said.

articles.title: A delivery company founded by Arabs takes on its competition in Israel
articles.summary: Deep inside the labyrinthine alleys of Acre’s Old City – home to a 700-year-old Crusader fortress – Muhammad Hani could not order a takeaway pizza. Delivery drivers struggled to navigate the maze of tightly packed ancient buildings, narrow alleyways and winding streets – leaving many of the Arab citizens of Israel there cut off from such services.
articles.body: Deep inside the labyrinthine alleys of Acre’s Old City – home to a 700-year-old Crusader fortress – Muhammad Hani could not order a takeaway pizza. Delivery drivers struggled to navigate the maze of tightly packed ancient buildings, narrow alleyways and winding streets – leaving many of the Arab citizens of Israel there cut off from such services. “Only the residents like us know how to get around these neighborhoods,” the 27-year-old said. And even if a driver could find the house address, another barrier remained. Many Arab citizens could only pay with cash, while delivery companies such as Wolt, the leading operator in Israel, only accept card payments. “Most people here don’t have a bank card,” Hani explained. Launched in 2019, Haat set out to tackle some of the barriers that left communities like Hani’s on the margins of Israel’s high-tech society. Not everyone in the country known as the “Startup Nation” could reap the rewards of cutting-edge services from the latest applications. At first, the idea for Haat was simple: combine technology with the old-fashioned convenience of cash. But the technology ultimately found uses far beyond its initial goal, helping the Israeli postal service map villages and allowing small, local restaurants to grow a customer base far beyond their neighborhoods. Founded by Hasan Abasi in the Arab-majority town of Umm al-Fahm in Israel, Haat now offers its services across 50 cities, working with more than 10,000 restaurants and markets, and employing more than 500 couriers. Its success has earned the app a valuation of more than $100 million, according to the company’s PR and Communications lead, Aida Kaddan. Abasi’s creative strategy with Haat also helped him nab a place on Globes’ 40 Under 40, an annual list by one of Israel’s leading business newspapers recognizing promising young Israelis. Abasi came up with Haat – Arabic for “bring” – while working for Google in Switzerland. The 36-year-old returned to Umm al-Fahm from Zurich as his wife was expecting a second child. One evening, he tried to order a pizza, but the courier kept getting lost. The experience helped Abasi recognize a wider problem – and an opportunity. He launched Haat with five others, starting in Umm al-Fahm before expanding to neighboring Arab towns. Demand exploded during the Covid-19 pandemic, when lockdowns kept people at home and online orders boomed. Abasi was also aware of the systemic issues around banking in Israel, particularly in the Arab sector, where, according to a 2024 study from The National Insurance Institute of Israel, more than 37% live in poverty. Many lower-income families simply don’t have electronic payment options, especially in Umm al-Fahm, according to Mayor Samir Mahamed, making cash the most convenient form of payment. Like a ‘90s Domino’s delivery Haat combined the convenience of shopping and dining through a smart phone application with an old-school pay-by-cash option. This option proved useful beyond Arab communities and has caught on in mixed neighborhoods like Jaffa, where many people do not have bank cards, Kaddan said. Haat has since expanded its services to allow users also to pay utility and phone bills with cash. “The cash option came from answering the needs of the society. It has now become one of Haat’s most significant advantages in every area where it operates,” she said. As Haat focused on reaching those underserved by other delivery applications, its work to turn previously unnavigable streets into mapped-out towns advanced. Uncharted territory In some Arab neighbourhoods in Israel, not only were the maze of densely built homes a challenge for delivery services, but streets also often lacked formal names or had unnumbered houses. “Navigation relied heavily on neighborhood names, family compounds and local landmarks, which posed considerable challenges for postal distribution, commercial deliveries and emergency services,” said Mahamed, the Umm al-Fahm mayor. Over the past six years, Haat has helped redraw the map of underserved cities. By tracking courier routes and using machine learning to identify roads, neighborhoods, buildings and entrance points overlooked by conventional navigation services, the company says its maps now include 30% more streets in the areas it serves than other mapping platforms. This was particularly useful for residents in Umm al-Faham, a city of more than 57,000. The mayor said Haat helped support a city-wide project carried out by the local authority to name streets and number houses. CNN has reached out to Israel’s postal service for comment. Beyond word-of-mouth The improved access to Arab neighborhoods also opened up new markets for restaurants and shops overlooked by the wider community, something Haat said “democratizes visibility.” Krunchy Chicken began as a single fried chicken restaurant in Baqa al-Gharbiyye, an Arab town in northern Israel near the border with the occupied West Bank. The restaurant has since opened two more branches in the Israeli Triangle – a concentration of Arab towns and villages on the Green Line, which demarcates the boundary between the West Bank and Israel. At first, Krunchy Chicken relied largely on word-of-mouth advertising, according to manager Sharif Masarweh. But the online exposure of Haat helped greatly, Masarweh told CNN, as did the convenience of different payment options. “The fact that there is an option for cash also allowed more people to use the application and to order food from our restaurant and others. It helped a lot, because not everyone prefers to pay using a bank card,” he said. Haat recently expanded into Tel Aviv, taking on Finland’s Wolt, the dominant player in Israel’s food delivery market. Wolt motorbikes zipping along the streets and weaving through dense traffic are an ubiquitous sight in the beachside city. Now the local competitor is trying to build its own foothold in Tel Aviv using its strengths. “Haat reads the needs of local people because we are local and operate from within,” Kaddan said. “We see what is missing and try to fill those gaps with technology.”

articles.title: In 2007, a California engineer set out by bicycle and rowboat to circle Earth alone; five years later, he returned after 41,196 miles and three ocean crossings powered only by himself
articles.summary: US News: In 2007, Erden Eruç embarked on a five-year journey to complete the world's first human-powered solo circumnavigation of Earth. His adventure included crossing three oceans and covering over 41,196 miles entirely by bicycle and rowboat.
articles.body: On 10 July 2007, Seattle-based engineer Erden Eruç set out from a pier in Bodega Bay, California, to complete the first solo circumnavigation of the globe using human power, a journey that, according to Guinness World Records, involved rowing, kayaking, hiking, and cycling. Post Alley reports that he cashed out his 401(k) to fund the expedition, while Back in America describes the boat in detail.Erden Eruç arrived back at the same pier in Bodega Bay, California, on 21 July 2012, completing what Guinness World Records recognizes as the first solo circumnavigation of the globe using human power. Guinness World Records puts the journey at 5 years, 11 days, 12 hours, and 22 minutes, covering a total distance of 66,299 km (41,196 miles). He is recorded as the first person to complete a solo human-powered circumnavigation, and he was also the first to row across the three oceans: the Pacific Ocean, the Indian Ocean, and the Atlantic Ocean. Below are the route, followed by two research papers that offer context on what ocean rowing demands of the body.The route: Bodega Bay to Bodega Bay, 10 July 2007 to 21 July 2012Post Alley traces Eruç's route up to about the halfway point of the expedition. He rowed from California to Australia, where he cycled across the country and climbed Mount Kosciuszko, the highest peak on the continent. From there, he rowed across the Indian Ocean to Tanzania and climbed Kilimanjaro. After this, he cycled to Namibia. Guinness World Records covers the Atlantic leg. Eruç rowed from Lüderitz, Namibia, to Güiria, Venezuela, and then cycled to Carúpano, Venezuela. He next crossed the Gulf of Mexico to Cameron, Louisiana, USA, arriving on 27 May 2012. Finally, he cycled to reach Bodega Bay.Eruç used a rowing boat on the ocean, a bicycle on land, and kayaks along the coastlines. The initial circumnavigation by Eruç took about five years, with lengthy stops in between for repairs and planning the next step in the journey. Although the total duration is well documented, there is no exact, reliable figure for how many of those days were spent traveling and how many were spent resting.49 transatlantic rowers and a 10% loss of body massNo study has followed Eruç himself, but research on transatlantic rowers suggests what a single ocean crossing can demand of the body. The paper Maximal sustainable energy intake during transatlantic ocean rowing is insufficient for total energy expenditure and skeletal muscle mass maintenance appeared in Experimental Physiology in November 2023. The Experimental Physiology paper reports data from 49 rowers (32 males and 17 females, ages 24-67 years) who took part in the Talisker Whisky Atlantic Challenge, with complete datasets from 25 rowers in 2020 and 24 in 2021. According to the paper, the rowers worked in a continuous pattern of two- to three-hour shifts, 24 hours a day, for a minimum of 12 hours of rowing daily. The race covers roughly 3,000 miles, and typical race durations in the paper range from about 40 to 59 days, with the rowers in this study averaging 46 days at sea.Energy expenditure was determined using the doubly labeled water technique during the last week of participation in the challenge. Energy expenditure was 2.5-fold higher than the resting metabolic rate in males and 2.3-fold in females; energy intake was equal for both groups. Nevertheless, there was a significant reduction in body mass in both groups, by 10.2% in males and 10.0% in females. Thus, the scientists conclude that sustainable energy intake in a rower is less than the energy expenditure and energy needs of the skeletal muscles.A 37-year-old's 38-day solo row across the North Atlantic in 2018The paper The Physical and Psychological Experience of Rowing the North Atlantic Solo and Unassisted was published in Wilderness and Environmental Medicine in 2020. It followed one 37-year-old man who left St. John's, Newfoundland, on 27 June 2018. He traveled roughly 2,000 miles (3,218 km) over 38 days, 6 hours and 49 minutes before arriving at the Isles of Scilly. He scored each day regarding his effort, physical feelings, and mood. Daily ratings of perceived effort, body sensations, and mood were collected during the crossing to assess its progress, transforming one athlete's experience into an insight into the physical and psychological difficulties of unsupported ocean crossing. The research being a case study, the results obtained can only serve as an illustration and not be generalized, but nevertheless provide a unique daily account of how difficult the crossing really was.A hurricane named Chris prevented him from rowing for 8 days, and a normal rowing day saw him rowing for 10 to 11 hours. His ratings for pain, loneliness, boredom, anxiety, and frustration remained low on average, while fatigue, restfulness, positive affect, calmness, and confidence were moderate. The study adds that only 16 people had completed the transatlantic row, while 31 attempts had failed, three of them ending with the rowers lost at sea. Because the study features a single rower, it cannot stand in as a profile of Eruç; it serves only as context for what a long solo ocean crossing can involve. However, Guinness World Records shows his row between Lüderitz and Guiria from 10 October 2011 to 11 March 2012 as the record for the longest nonstop distance rowed across the Atlantic at 5,788 miles. This is almost twice the distance of the transatlantic row in the above mentioned Experimental Physiology study, and over 3 times the time spent at sea.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Two dead in Moscow as Ukraine launches massive drone attack while Russia votes
articles.summary: The largest Ukrainian drone attack reported so far on the Moscow region killed two people ⁠and damaged part of an oil refinery in the capital, authorities said Sunday.
articles.body: MOSCOW — Ukraine launched what Moscow’s mayor called the biggest drone attack yet on the Russian capital on Sunday, as Russians voted on the final day of a parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for the war in ⁠Ukraine. The drone strikes killed two people in the Moscow region and two more in the Russian-held part of Ukraine’s Kherson region, including an election official, according to Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin and election authorities. A facility at Moscow’s oil refinery, which has been targeted before, was also damaged. “The biggest attack by enemy drones has been repelled,” Sobyanin said on Telegram. “This unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed.” Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram: “In the Moscow region tonight, our long-range responses hit very noticeably. One of the key enterprises of Russia’s oil industry and an aggressor logistics facility were struck.” He added that Moscow should “end its brutal war and choose peace.” The State Duma vote, the first since Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine ⁠in February 2022, is expected to see the ruling United Russia party easily retain ​its ⁠dominance in a political system critics say does not tolerate dissent. The Kremlin is likely to present the outcome as evidence of public backing for Putin’s policies and for the war, now in its fifth year with no sign of ending soon. The election authorities say the ⁠three days of voting have proceeded smoothly despite cyberattacks reported on Saturday. Turnout by late morning on Sunday was at over 45% for the ​Duma vote and ⁠regional elections, said Central Election Commission Chairwoman Ella Pamfilova. Most anti-war ‌candidates have been barred from the ballot. Those who did run from the liberal Yabloko party, which has polled in the single digits in recent years but hoped to tap into war fatigue, said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the ‌vote for comments about the conflict. Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake ‌news is punishable by lengthy prison sentences. In a small act of defiance, Yabloko’s leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrably spoiled his ballot paper, writing his party’s name and the slogan “For peace”. The Kremlin says national unity and some censorship are necessary during what it calls its special military operation in Ukraine. It casts the conflict — Europe’s deadliest since World War Two — as part of an existential struggle with a ⁠hostile West. Moscow says Ukrainian intelligence services and other enemies are stepping up efforts to stir unrest inside Russia. Russian electoral officials said on Saturday that an online voting system in Moscow had come under cyberattack. Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a “pseudo election”. Putin on Friday also accused Ukraine of trying to interfere in the election, citing what he said was a Ukrainian strike that killed an election official in her home in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region on Tuesday. Reuters could not independently verify details of the attack and there was no comment from Kyiv. Despite what experts see as the election’s predictable outcome, the NEST think-tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, said the vote could ‌still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain. “The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the ​country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on ‌the ballot,” it said in a note. It said the Communist Party and the New People Party could attract votes the authorities would prefer to go to United Russia. Both parties have consistently voted in ⁠line with United Russia on major issues. Putin told the nation in a televised address before the election that the vote would underline support for Russian troops fighting in Ukraine. “Your choice, and your will, ‌will once again demonstrate that millions of people stand ​behind our soldiers, that we are a united people bound together by shared ‌values, historical memory, and love for our homeland, and that no ​one will succeed in dividing or intimidating us,” said Putin. Initial results are expected to start emerging at around 2pm ET on Sunday, with more complete results available on Monday.

articles.title: Folkestone council evacuates nearby residents after Grand Burstin hotel fire
articles.summary: Residents living near Folkestone’s Grand Burstin Hotel relocated after safety inspectors' concerns.
articles.body:
Residents living near to a fire-damaged seaside hotel in Folkestone have been evacuated over safety fears that the intensity of the basement blaze weakened the building's structure, the council has said.

The blaze broke out at the Grand Burstin Hotel in Marine Parade in the early hours of Saturday, with about 280 people evacuated.

Folkestone and Hythe District Council said 90 people were relocated from Pavilion Court in Marine Terrace following concerns raised by safety inspectors.

Kent Police said the blaze was being treated as suspicious and has appealed for witnesses.

A council spokesperson said the Pavilion Court residents had been given hotel accommodation in the town, adding that it was "working to arrange alternative housing for all affected residents while the Grand Burstin undergoes further assessments and any required works to make it safe".

In a statement, Britannia Hotels Group, which runs the Grand Burstin, said it was "fully cooperating with Kent Police and supporting their investigation into the circumstances surrounding the fire".

It added: "We remain in close contact with all relevant authorities and will provide any assistance or information required as their enquiries continue.

"In the meantime, the safety and wellbeing of our guests and team members remains our priority."

A total of 26 fire engines were sent to the hotel at about 01:05 BST on Saturday, Kent Fire & Rescue Service said, adding: "It's believed the fire started in the basement of the property."

On Sunday morning, one fire engine remained at the scene monitoring for hotspots.

Station manager Lawrence Pater said the "very severe" fire had raised concerns about the structural integrity of the building and that the fire service was seeking advice from inspectors.

Folkestone & Hythe District Council set up a welfare centre at the Three Hills Sports Park for hotel residents evacuated on Saturday.

Other local businesses, including nearby pub The Harbour Inn, also opened their doors to those affected.

The council's chief executive, Susan Priest, said: "The extent of support of organisations, including Three Hills, Morrisons and the Salvation Army, has been amazing and helped to ensure that visitors and residents were looked after, supported and had food and hot drinks.

"This was an extremely difficult day, firstly for the hotel guests and this evening for our residents who have had to move out of their homes."

Ross Honeycomb, 39, was staying at the hotel with his family and told the BBC on Saturday how they were woken by fire alarms at about 01:00.

He said: "I thought I was dreaming, it was horrifying.

"We looked out and there was smoke billowing from the underground car park. Later we started hearing explosions."

Kevin Crawford, 91, and his wife Kathleen, 82, said they had booked in for a two-week stay at the hotel.

The couple, from London, told the BBC that they were in their room on the sixth floor when they heard a fire alarm.

"We saw the fire but we thought the fire brigade had it under control," said Kevin.

"We managed to sleep through it. At the time, we didn't realise how bad the fire was."

articles.title: Germany’s Friedrich Merz under pressure as far-right AfD eye more regional election gains
articles.summary: German voters go to the polls on Sunday in two state elections that look likely to heap more pressure on struggling Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose future has been in the balance since the far right’s triumph in another regional vote this month.
articles.body: BERLIN — German voters go to the polls on Sunday in two state elections that look likely to heap more pressure on struggling Chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose future has been in the balance since the far right’s triumph in another regional vote this month. The ⁠elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a largely rural state in the formerly communist east, and the capital Berlin follow the September 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) came close to the rare feat of winning an absolute majority. Regional elections would not usually draw much interest outside Germany, but the AfD’s success in Saxony-Anhalt, which it sees as the first step towards winning federal elections due in 2029, has sent shock waves through Europe. In just over a decade, the party, which ⁠wants to take tough action to deport foreigners with no right to stay in ​Germany, restore ⁠energy ties with Russia and quit the euro, has transformed itself from a fringe eurosceptic movement to the country’s most popular party. Opinion polls indicate it is unlikely to repeat its victory in Saxony-Anhalt in either of Sunday’s votes. But they are both expected to ⁠underscore the huge advances it has made in recent years and raise fresh questions over the so-called “firewall” strategy, under which the other main ​parties refuse ⁠to enter coalition agreements with it. For Merz, whose approval ratings ‌have plunged as low as 14%, according to the latest polls, the result was the latest in a series of blows that have raised growing doubts in his own conservative Christian Democratic Union party about whether he can continue to lead. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the CDU looks likely to suffer ‌its worst-ever election result, with the most recent opinion poll by the Forschungsgruppe Wahlen on ‌Friday putting it at just 6% and at risk of failing to clear the minimum threshold to enter the state parliament. Merz has struggled Elected last year on a promise of ambitious reforms to return Germany’s stagnant economy to growth, Merz has struggled to win over sceptical voters, compounding resentment over unpopular pension, tax and healthcare reforms with a stream of gaffes and communication missteps. For the ⁠moment at least, senior figures in the CDU have rallied behind him, aware that replacing the chancellor — which would in any case be difficult on constitutional grounds — would leave any successor facing the same deep economic problems. But disillusionment with his government has hung over the campaigns in both Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, where voters have focused on issues including soaring energy and housing costs. Surging fuel prices, felt acutely in a state like Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania where many rely on cars for transport, have put pressure on Merz to agree relief measures with his Social Democrat coalition partners. On Friday, he presented a relief package that included tax cuts on gas and diesel. In the rural state, polls have shown the race narrowing over recent weeks as the centre-left ‌Social Democrats (SPD) have centred their campaign around popular state premier Manuela Schwesig. The Wahlen poll on Friday showed the SPD edging ​in front of the AfD for the first time in months. The poll put the SPD on 37%, the AfD on 36%, ‌the far-left Left Party on 9% and the environmental Greens on ⁠5%, just at the threshold for entering parliament. Both parties would be potential coalition partners for Schwesig. In Berlin, the Wahlen poll showed ⁠the far-left Left Party moving ahead of the CDU, threatening the conservative hold on the mayor’s office in a campaign that has focused heavily on housing affordability. Even in liberal Berlin, however, ‌the AfD has made strong gains, moving ​into third place. The latest poll puts the Left Party on 22%, the ‌CDU on 20%, the Greens on 15% and the SPD on ​12%. The AfD sits on 18%, while the far-left BSW, the only party that has said it might agree to work with the AfD, is just under the parliamentary threshold on 4%.

articles.title: Alleged killer mom Corie Walsh ruled too dangerous to return home — but psychiatrist warns risk can change
articles.summary: Forensic psychiatrist explains why a dangerousness finding isn't permanent for Corie Walsh, the Illinois mother held without pretrial release.
articles.body: An Illinois judge found Corie Walsh too dangerous to release after prosecutors alleged the Frankfort mother posed a threat to her husband and three surviving children after she was charged with murdering her 2-year-old son, Barrett. But forensic psychiatrists say "dangerousness" is not a permanent label. Instead, it is a forward-looking assessment that can change as a person's mental condition improves through treatment. Walsh, 40, remains held without pretrial release after a Will County judge denied her request to leave custody during a detention hearing earlier this month. LINDSAY CLANCY FIXATION AND ALLEGED PLOT TO POISON HUSBAND EMERGE AS ACCUSED MOM CLAIMS PSYCHOSIS The judge also ordered that Walsh immediately receive psychiatric medication after her attorneys said she had gone days without treatment despite a hospital recommendation that she receive around-the-clock psychiatric care. Prosecutors argued Walsh should remain behind bars because, beyond the allegations surrounding Barrett's death, she allegedly threatened to kill her husband after her arrest. The judge agreed, finding Walsh posed too great a danger to release before trial. LINDSAY CLANCY’S FUTURE COULD REST WITH ‘PROSECUTION DOCTORS’ AS CASE ECHOES INFAMOUS MAINE KILLINGS: EXPERT The ruling raised a broader question that extends beyond Walsh's case: What does it actually mean when a judge determines someone is too dangerous to release? Under Illinois law, judges deciding whether a defendant should remain jailed before trial evaluate the person's current risk to others rather than punish past conduct. Dr. Stephen Dinwiddie, a professor of psychiatry at Northwestern University with four decades of forensic psychiatry experience, said psychiatrists approach dangerousness the same way – as a forward-looking assessment rather than a permanent label. VIRGINIA MAN ACQUITTED BY INSANITY IN KILLING FLEES US DURING 48-HOUR MENTAL HOSPITAL PASS "Obviously we're talking more about what we're afraid they're going to do tomorrow," he said. "Part of that prediction is based on what they did yesterday ... what they did in the past ... and what they have said they intend to do." Unlike a criminal verdict, which looks backward at what allegedly happened, dangerousness is designed to evaluate the risk a person may pose going forward, Dinwiddie said. "It's pretty squishy," he said. "Dangerous to whom? Imminently or long-term? Dangerous in a physical way or something else?" In civil commitment proceedings, judges often decide whether someone should receive treatment over their objections because they present a short-term danger to themselves or others. Dinwiddie said the rationale is simple: "If we don't act, something bad is going to happen within a matter of days, if not sooner." Dinwiddie said treatment can dramatically change how psychiatrists evaluate a person's future risk. SCOTT WOLF'S WIFE SAYS ‘MY BRAIN TURNED ON ME’ AS SHE APOLOGIZES TO FAMILY FOR 'PROFOUND HARM' AFTER PSYCHOSIS "If they've behaved in a violent fashion while ill in the past and now they're ill, obviously that's important information and obviously that's something to worry about," he said. "The intervention obviously is to try to get at that particular symptom of illness and get it under control." That can have legal significance because Illinois judges may reconsider detention if circumstances materially change, although any decision to release a defendant before trial remains up to the court. "I think most of us believe that our interventions can prevent tragedies," Dinwiddie said. articles.title: Florida plastic surgeon accused of killing attorney in his office defends himself in murder trial
articles.summary: Tomasz Kosowski represents himself in a death penalty trial for the alleged murder of attorney Steven Cozzi, whose body was never recovered.
articles.body: An unusual trial is underway for a Florida plastic surgeon, accused of murdering an attorney he’d opposed in court and disposing of his body in a dumpster before prosecutors say it ended up at the landfill. Clad in an orange jail jumpsuit, Dr. Tomasz Kosowski, 47, is representing himself in court as he faces a first-degree murder charge with the possibility of the death penalty. He’s waived his right to a jury – the judge presiding over the Pinellas County trial is set to decide the doctor’s fate. Kosowski was arrested in March 2023 in connection with the disappearance of attorney Steven Cozzi. He has remained in jail and insists he is innocent. The two men met through a legal dispute. FLORIDA PLASTIC SURGEON MAY HAVE MURDERED MISSING LAWYER IN LAW FIRM BATHROOM: POLICE Cozzi had worked on a civil lawsuit beginning in 2019 involving money allegedly owed to Kosowski for work he’d done tied to personal injury cases. Cozzi helped represent the corporate clients Kosowski was suing. During years of litigation, Kosowski developed a hostile attitude toward Cozzi, according to court records. He blamed Cozzi for his problems in the case and demanded that the attorney be removed as defense counsel, records show. "He made a bunch of completely unwarranted, inappropriate accusations about Steve throughout the litigation," said Jake Pillsbury, an attorney who worked with Cozzi on the case. Cozzi had told others that, during a deposition, Kosowski approached him in a restroom and "called him a scumbag" and "that he [Kosowski] was going to win," Pillsbury said in court. Those close to Cozzi began to worry about his safety. Cozzi’s husband, Michael Montgomery, had suggested arranging for "some kind of on-site security," if Cozzi had to meet with Kosowski again. Blood-spattered discovery On March 21, 2023, Cozzi and Kosowski both were scheduled to attend a teleconference hearing at 10 a.m. Before that, it was a normal Tuesday morning, Montgomery said. Cozzi brought him his morning coffee and they had a short conversation before he left for work. That was the last time he’d see him. About 10 minutes before the meeting, Cozzi left his phone, keys, wallet, and other items on his desk and went to the office restroom. He never showed up for the scheduled teleconference. NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS Later, Cozzi’s boss entered the restroom and found spattered blood, court records show. Security footage from the day Cozzi disappeared shows a subject arriving in a silver Toyota Tundra around 8:30 a.m. The prosecution alleges it was Kosowski. A man wearing dark gloves entered the building where Cozzi worked carrying a box "large enough to conceal a human body," according to investigators. At 10:22 a.m., the same man exited the building pulling a wagon covered with a reddish orange blanket. The man could be seen struggling with the weight of the cart while pulling it to the truck, records show. SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS That day, the Tundra was driven to Kosowski’s home in Tarpon Springs, Florida, videos pieced together from multiple surveillance cameras showed, according to court records. On the way, the truck passed a Flock camera that captured an image of "a red bag or blanket in a cart that appeared to contain what resembles a human body located in the bed of the truck," according to arrest records. Two days later, investigators arrived at Kosowski’s home with a search warrant and found the Tundra in the garage with blood in the truck bed, on the driver’s side headrest, on the driver’s side floorboard and on the garage floor. Cozzi’s DNA was found in the Tundra and Kosowski’s garage floor, court records show. SEND US A TIP In the search of Kosowski’s vehicles, investigators found a ballistic vest with a "substantial amount" of blood on it. They also found one iPhone and a "burner phone"––the term for an inexpensive, prepaid device meant to be discarded. Law enforcement officials also found a vest meant to be worn by a medical first responder, sheriff's office patches, a foldable bike, a gas can, $282,000 in cash, two passports and black, industrial-sized garbage bags. Investigators also found a black duffel that the prosecution has called "a murder bag." Inside, there were lighters, a Taser, scissors, brass knuckles, a crowbar, ski masks and a Guy Fawkes mask. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST The bag also contained a syringe, a needle and a vial of succinylcholine, a paralytic drug. It was labeled in a way that connected it to Kosowski’s plastic-surgery office in Miami. Surprising maneuvers caught on video After Kosowski was arrested, police informed him they’d be searching his body to collect possible DNA and fingernail clippings, and would be taking photographs of him, the prosecution said. After that, camera footage from inside the patrol car shows Kosowski struggling to bring his hands from behind his back, underneath his feet and up to his face. He then began to "meticulously suck on each of his fingers," a member of the prosecution team told the judge. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL "He's using his tongue and getting up underneath it and slurping. He's using his teeth almost as a nail file, trying to destroy any trace of evidence that might bring him back to Steven Cozzi." The prosecution argues that Kosowski began planning the killing long before he allegedly murdered Cozzi. More than a month before the attorney’s disappearance, Kosowski allegedly visited Cozzi’s home without his knowledge and photographed a car in the carport, according to the prosecution team. Kosowski also visited Blanchard Law Firm where Cozzi worked. He drove around the building and took photos multiple times before Cozzi’s disappearance, the prosecution has alleged. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X In early March 2023, Kosowski began searching Cozzi and Montgomery online, seeking information about their wedding and records about previous and current addresses, prosecutors said. An employee of the building that housed the Blanchard Law Firm told investigators that a week before Cozzi’s disappearance, she found a man in a mask hiding in the office utility closet. Suspicious, she asked him why he was there, court records show. He told her it was because of a power outage and walked away. She watched him leave in a grey Toyota Tundra, investigators said. Fingerprints matching Kosowski’s were later found in that closet. Investigators never found Cozzi’s body. Searching for Cozzi On the day Cozzi disappeared, Kosowski’s cellphone was allegedly tracked traveling toward his second home in Miami. He pulled off on a dirt road in South Florida near the Everglades where there’s a dumpster, court records show. Records of his cellphone’s location show he returned to the dumpster two days later, the prosecution alleges. The team argues that Kosowski returned to the garbage collection container to see if it had been emptied. Law enforcement later investigated the dumpster and a K-9 trained in human detection alerted on it, indicating the presence of human remains. But a body was not found. Investigators tracked down the garbage truck driver who collected that dumpster on his route. He remembers that day. "It was a smell that he had never experienced," a member of the prosecution team told the court. "He described that smell as vile. He had to crush the trash back in his garbage truck so many times, because the stench was so overwhelming––and this is someone who is a garbage truck driver." The day he drove that load, the garbage truck driver stopped at a store to buy air freshener because he "could not stand the scent that was in his nose while he was driving around," the prosecution said. That smell was "Steven's body decaying in the Florida heat for two days." Video captured by a camera mounted on the garbage truck captured the load from the dumpster tumbling into the truck. That footage shows "a lot of black industrial-sized garbage bags, similar to the ones that Dr. Kozowski had in the trunk of his car," a prosecution team member told the judge. Video shown in court shows bags falling into the truck that are "consistent with a human body," the prosecution team said. Law enforcement officers visited the landfill where the garbage truck dumped that load, but it was more than a week after it was deposited. By that time, more than 6,000 tons of compacted garbage had been piled atop the load. GOT A TIP? Still, in an attempt to recover the body of Cozzi, they sifted through the landfill for days, officers testified in court. "His hearse was a dump truck, and his burial site… is at the Collier County Landfill," a prosecutor told the court. The prosecution team has called dozens of witnesses to testify before Judge Joseph Bulone. In July 2025, a written plea of not guilty was submitted by an attorney representing Kosowski at the time. In that plea, he requested a trial by jury. More than a year later, on Aug. 31, Kosowski told the court he’d changed his mind and wanted a judge to decide his fate. His trialbegan on Sept. 14. LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE For the first three days of the trial, Kosowski sat mostly quiet, blandly staring at witnesses, taking notes and giving short answers to questions from the judge. On the fourth day, he began cross-examining some of the prosecution’s witnesses who had presented evidence. He has objected to evidence obtained from his body, from his Toyota Corolla and from his residence, according to court records. His motions to suppress the evidence were denied. On Sept. 18, the fifth day of his trial, he asked the judge to strike a key witness’s testimony about DNA evidence. He argued that the witness, a DNA expert, didn’t provide enough of his own interpretation of the numbers. Bulone denied the motion, but said Kosowski could challenge the DNA findings in closing arguments. Fox News Digital was not able to reach Kosowski for comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The trial is set to resume on Sept. 22.

articles.title: Lib Dem Daisy Cooper vows to end 'computer says no' economy to boost growth
articles.summary: Deputy leader Daisy Cooper also proposes a Growth and Defence Partnership with the EU in a speech to her party conference.
articles.body:
Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper has warned the UK's economic growth is being held back by a "computer says no" approach.

She unveiled a 30-page growth plan aimed at removing barriers to business as part of her speech to the Lib Dem conference in Brighton.

Cooper, who is also the party's Treasury spokesperson, said too many ideas, start-ups and research started in Britain but ended up being taken overseas.

She also outlined a new Growth and Defence Partnership with the EU to reverse the economic damage of Brexit, that she claimed is currently costing the UK £90bn a year in lost tax revenue.

Speaking on stage in Brighton, she said: "We build brilliant start-ups, and watch too many leave to scale somewhere else. We produce world-class research, and too little of it becomes a British product."

"Britain has the potential," she went on. "The system holds it back. The computer says no.

"This plan tears down the barriers to investment, to innovation, and to skills."

Cooper called for the creation of a digital one-stop-shop service for businesses and investors, combining tax, regulatory, legal, Companies House, and general business services.

Creating this within a new Department for Growth would simplify red tape and help small and medium-sized businesses compete and grow, she said.

Cooper said a new Growth and Defence Partnership with the EU, would be the "single biggest growth lever we could pull" by deepening ties with Europe.

"It could turbo-charge our economy and start to reverse the economic damage of Brexit which is currently costing us £90bn a year in lost tax revenue," she said.

"In power, we will strike the deal on the single market, we will strike the deal on a customs union, we will strike the deal on defence."

She claimed the Lib Dems would say "what no other party dares to say" that Britain "belongs at the heart of Europe, and we will take her there."

Before becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham said he would like to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime but he respected the result of the 2016 referendum and had no plans to "re-run" Brexit arguments .

On Friday, Chancellor John Healey met EU ministers and asked them to let the UK into its Made in Europe scheme , aimed at protecting industries from unfair Chinese competition.

Healey also pushed for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin the same day, as Burnham held his first official meeting with Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) Micheál Martin in No 10 North.

Seeking to differentiate the Liberal Democrats from rival parties, she said her party would avoid "more punishing tax hikes from Labour or painful spending cuts by the Conservatives and Reform UK".

She attacked Healey for his speech earlier this month , which "contained no vision, no ideas, and absolutely no mention of Europe".

Cooper also attacked Reform and the Conservatives for being "locked in a race to the bottom without a single credible costing between them".

She highlighted how the new Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith had helped to deliver and defend the Liz Truss mini-budget, which she said "crashed the pound, it spiked your mortgage, it cost the country billions", and Nigel Farage defended the move.

"But the worst could be yet to come: Farage is modelling himself on Trump," she said.

"A President who has used the presidency to enrich himself, dismantled anti-corruption safeguards and pardoned crypto criminals.

"We cannot allow that kind of politics to take hold in our country -- We cannot afford to allow Nigel Farage to win the keys to No 10 or let the Tories put him there."

articles.title: King Charles accused of ‘gaslighting’ by Princess Diana’s brother in dispute over book claims
articles.summary: Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, has accused King Charles of “gaslighting” him after Buckingham Palace pushed back at his claims about the monarch’s conduct.
articles.body: Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, has accused King Charles of “gaslighting” him after Buckingham Palace pushed back at his claims about the monarch’s conduct. Buckingham Palace released an unusually forceful statement Wednesday ahead of the release of a memoir by Spencer, which charts the breakdown of then-Prince Charles’s marriage to Princess Diana, and the fallout from her death in a Paris car crash in 1997, one year after the royal couple finalized their divorce. In an initial excerpt released ahead of publication, Spencer recalled a heated phone call with Charles amid a disagreement about funeral arrangements, claiming that a furious Charles had told him Diana would “soon be forgotten.” “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” the palace had responded. In an interview with Britain’s Mail on Sunday newspaper, Spencer said: “It is not every day you wake up to find you’ve been gaslit by the king.” “It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the king being able to deny what I’d said,” Spencer added. “Gaslighting” is a form of manipulation where the manipulator is trying to get someone to question their own reality, memory or perceptions. Spencer also denied he was motivated by money in publishing the book, saying it “has never even been the remotest consideration” and stressing that “my primary responsibility as a historian is to tell the truth.” The aristocrat, an earl whose family has generational ties with Britain’s royal family, has made a number of other allegations in excerpts since released from the book, published in advance by the Daily Mail newspaper. In the excerpts, Spencer writes that Charles sounded “giddily elated” and “like a lottery winner” when they spoke by phone immediately after Diana’s death, adding: “I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not.” He also speaks about his sister’s mental health and recounts conversations with her, recalling that she had told him how “things became very difficult indeed in the marriage early on.” Spencer’s book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is due to be released publicly on Tuesday. Since its initial statement, Buckingham Palace has remained silent on the further allegations from Spencer’s book. NBC News attempted to seek further comment on Sunday, but the palace did not immediately respond. There has been no public comment from Princes William and Harry, Charles and Diana’s two sons, on Spencer’s memoir. Prince Harry, who quit as a working royal six years ago amid a reported rift with senior royals, has remained close to the Spencer family, with his own memoir “Spare” thanking “my mother’s siblings for their love, support, time, and perspective.” In an interview with the BBC that is set to air Sunday, Spencer said that Harry and his wife Megan Markle’s treatment at the hands of Britain’s infamous tabloid press has “echoes” of what happened to Diana. “If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant,” Spencer said when questioned whether he believed Diana would “identify” with the scrutiny faced by Harry and Megan. He added: “I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana’s example. I’m not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who’s being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life.” The royal family continued to undertake public duties this week even as Spencer’s book has dominated the headlines, with Charles also meeting with senior figures in AI at a summit in Scotland.
